prompt_text:
The figure contrasts the natural salt cycle with a human-altered salt cycle across a connected landscape of mountains, rivers, soils, groundwater, coasts, and the atmosphere. In the natural system, salts are released slowly by rock weathering, moved by rivers and groundwater, exchanged in soils, cycled through plants and organisms, and concentrated near coasts by evaporation, sea spray, and occasional seawater intrusion. Atmospheric transport and deposition redistribute marine salts inland, while sedimentation and geologic uplift store and later re-expose salts.

The lower panel shows how human activity intensifies and reroutes these same pathways. Agriculture, irrigation, road salt, fertilizer, mining, urbanization, pumping, and other industrial sources add extra salt to rivers, soils, and groundwater. Increased atmospheric dust and road-salt aerosols expand deposition from the air. Human-driven seawater intrusion and warming-enhanced evaporation increase salt accumulation in coastal and inland waters. Biological pathways are also altered through harvest, food trade, and fertilizer transport. Overall, the image emphasizes that the anthropogenic salt cycle is not a separate process but an amplification of the natural one, producing greater salt mobilization, faster transport, and broader contamination across environmental compartments.
